title: The chickpea in the pot
hookLine: a chickpea leaps from the boiling pot, and the cook says the heat is making it good (Masnavi 3.4158ff)

lines: A HARD YEAR YOU'RE GLAD OF.
cards: Think of the hardest year you've had that you're now, oddly, glad of. The first job where you knew nothing. The move to a city where you knew no one.
The year of the new baby, the long illness, the exam you had to retake. At the time it felt like being boiled alive. And yet something in you got softer, deeper, more you.
Rumi often reached for pictures from the kitchen, and he wrote about a small, hard, dried-out bean that did not want to be in the pot.

teach.h: A CHICKPEA LEAPS FROM THE POT.
teach.b: It's in Book Three of the Masnavi. Look at a chickpea in the pot, Rumi says, how it leaps up when the fire's lit. It keeps bobbing to the top, crying out: why are you setting me on fire?
You bought me, and now you're turning me upside down! The cook, a woman in Rumi's telling, keeps tapping it back down with her ladle. Boil nicely, she says.
Don't jump away from the one who lit the fire.

teach.h: I'M NOT BOILING YOU OUT OF DISLIKE.
teach.b: I'm not boiling you because I dislike you. It's so you'll get taste and flavor, so you can become food and mingle with life itself. Then she reminds the chickpea where it came from.
When you were green and fresh in the garden, you drank the rain. That drinking was for the sake of this fire. And in the end the chickpea says: all right, then.
If that's how it is, I'll boil gladly. Help me. Rumi is talking about the soul, and the hard things a person goes through on the way to God.
Sufis often speak of the raw and the cooked. A raw person is hard, dry, self-protective. A cooked one has been softened and made nourishing.
Be careful with this story, though. Rumi means the heat that ripens: effort, change, loss, long training. He isn't saying you should stay where someone is harming you and call it cooking.
Not all fire is a kitchen fire. But some of the heat in your life, the kind that's making you more patient, humbler, kinder, might be doing what the cook says.

how: In Sufi teaching, the path is often described as moving from raw to cooked, and stories like this are told to help people bear hard training and change with patience.

games.q: you're the chickpea. the water is boiling, and you've jumped to the top again. the cook explains the heat will give you flavor. what do you say?
o: all right; I'll boil gladly. help me.
I was happier in the garden.
games.why: in Rumi's telling, the chickpea agrees to boil gladly, and asks the cook for help.

practice: Let one difficulty come to mind that's stretching you, like a new role, a hard habit to build or a slow recovery; not the worst thing, and not anything where someone is hurting you. Feel the heat of it for a breath or two.
Then ask gently: what might this be softening in me?

wordCard.voice: Chickpea. It leaps from the boiling water, and the cook tells it the heat is giving it flavor and making it food. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian: a chickpea. Rumi's small, hard bean that learns to boil.

carryVoice: Your line: being cooked. Hard and dry going in, food coming out. That's day two hundred seven.
